value.overview: The Black-and-white Becard is a small, compact passerine of humid foothill and montane forests in Central and northern South America. It belongs to a group of canopy and understory insect-eating birds known for stout bills and distinctive, softly delivered songs. The species is uncommon to rare in parts of its range, including Costa Rica, where it is most often encountered in forested highlands and may be overlooked because it usually remains in dense vegetation.
value.classification: The Black-and-white Becard is a member of the family Tityridae, which includes becards, tityras, and related Neotropical birds. Its scientific name is Pachyramphus albogriseus.
value.identification: The male has a black crown and upperparts, a pale or white line above the eye, whitish underparts, and a graduated tail with white-tipped feathers. The female is generally more olive above and yellowish below, with a chestnut-colored crown bordered by darker feathers. It is a compact becard with a relatively large bill. In Costa Rica, careful attention is needed because several becard species can occur in similar forest habitats.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a disjunct distribution from Costa Rica and western Panama through parts of Colombia and Venezuela, with related taxonomic treatments differing over some South American populations. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly on the Caribbean slope from the Cordillera de Tilarán southward, generally in humid foothill and montane evergreen forest. It favors dense understory and forest interiors or edges at roughly 800–2,100 meters, although local records may extend beyond this range.
value.migrationStatus: The Black-and-white Becard is considered a year-round resident in Costa Rica rather than a long-distance migrant. Some individuals may make local or seasonal movements along elevational gradients, but regular migration out of the country is not established.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited. In Central America, nesting activity has been reported mainly from March through May. The nest is a bulky, roughly spherical structure made mostly from dead leaves, with moss and plant fibers, and has an entrance near the lower portion. It is usually placed in a vertical fork near the end of a branch several meters above the ground. Details such as clutch size, incubation, and fledging periods remain poorly documented.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of large insects and other arthropods, supplemented by small fruits. The bird usually forages alone or in pairs from the upper understory into the canopy. It takes prey or fruit from foliage and twigs, often making short fluttering sallies from a perch or briefly hovering at the end of a movement. It may also join mixed-species feeding flocks.
value.behavior: Black-and-white Becards are generally quiet and inconspicuous, often remaining within dense foliage. They are usually seen singly or in pairs and may participate briefly in mixed-species flocks. Males give a short, soft phrase of mellow notes, most often around dawn and during the early morning. Their compact shape, deliberate movements, and frequent short sallies from exposed perches are useful behavioral clues during observation.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population size has not been reliably quantified. Available assessments suggest that the population may be decreasing, but the scale and causes of any decline are uncertain.
